title: Trump Vows $5,000 Payments If GOP Holds Congress
summary:
During a Republican midterm convention speech in Dallas on Wednesday night, President Donald Trump promised a $5,000 dividend to every adult citizen if the Republican Party maintains control of Congress in the upcoming election. He did not explain where the money would come from during his more than 90-minute address.

According to the latest census data, implementing such payments could cost $1 trillion or more. Trump's speech covered his usual themes: tariffs (taxes on imported goods), dismantling Iran's nuclear program, and passing a bill to restrict voter identification and registration requirements. He also claimed inflation is lower than when he took office.

The speech came as several other major stories unfolded. In Missouri, Secretary of State Denny Hoskins faced the state Supreme Court on Thursday to explain why he should not be held in contempt. Hoskins is caught between two conflicting court rulings on a Republican redistricting plan that could influence the midterms. He chose to follow the ruling he preferred while ignoring his state's Supreme Court, which last week rejected the map that could help the GOP win a House seat.

Thursday also marked one year since a gunman fatally shot Charlie Kirk during a talk at Utah Valley University. Kirk founded Turning Point a little more than a decade before he died, aiming to engage young people in conservative politics. Over 10 years, he became a key figure among Generation Z and millennial conservatives. As supporters reflect, they describe a movement facing uncertainty about its future, struggling to rally around a new leader, and grappling with divisions affecting the broader Republican Party.

In other news, Apple's new CEO John Ternus unveiled a foldable device called iPhone Duo — the most radical change to the phone since it launched nearly 20 years ago. And pop star Olivia Rodrigo's Daisy Chain Fields festival raised $20 million for organizations supporting women and girls.
why_it_matters: The promise raises a core question in any democracy: who pays for what politicians promise, and whether a government can hand out money without raising taxes or borrowing more. Because Congress controls spending, the pledge also tests how much a single leader can really deliver — and whether voters believe it.

background_read: Payments straight from the government to ordinary citizens are unusual in the United States, but not unheard of. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Congress approved several rounds of stimulus checks that sent money to most American households, and Alaska (the northernmost state) has paid residents an annual dividend from its oil wealth for decades.

Under the Constitution it is Congress — not the president — that decides how federal money is spent, a power often called 'the power of the purse'. The U.S. government already spends far more than it collects in taxes and borrows the difference, so economists warn that a new trillion-dollar programme would add to that debt and could push prices up again.

Charlie Kirk (a conservative activist who founded Turning Point USA, a group that organises young conservatives on college campuses) was shot and killed at Utah Valley University (a public university in Utah), and his movement is now searching for a new leader. Generation Z (people born roughly between the late 1990s and the early 2010s) was the group Kirk aimed to reach.

perspectives.description: They see $5,000 per adult as direct help for families facing high grocery, rent and fuel bills, paid out of the country's wealth. For them it also motivates Republican voters to turn out in November.

They point out that no funding source was given and that $1 trillion or more would deepen the national debt or reignite inflation. Some also question whether tying cash to one party's victory puts a price tag on votes.

They note that big campaign promises are common and that Congress, not the president, holds the power of the purse. Direct payments do have precedents — pandemic stimulus checks in the United States and Alaska's annual oil dividend — but both were funded through specific laws.

If Republicans lose Congress, the promise disappears; if they keep it, a divided party would still have to pass a trillion-dollar bill. The real test may be whether the pledge changes turnout among voters who feel squeezed by prices.
